newsitem.title: ITALY: Iraq says U.S. "splitting hairs" over sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says U.S. "splitting hairs" over sanctions.

text.p: Iraq said on Saturday it had destroyed all weapons that needed to be destroyed and accused the United States of deliberately seeking to prolong U.N.-imposed trade sanctions against Baghdad.
"We believe we have abided by all our commitments to the (U.N.) Security Council," Iraqi Vice-President Taha Mohieddin Ma'rouf said at the World Food Summit.

He told a news conference there was no reason for the sanctions, imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, to continue and said they had driven his country into poverty. "Food should not be used as a weapon," he said.
He said the United States, which has blocked the Security Council from lifting or easing the sanctions, was "splitting hairs" over Iraq's compliance with U.N. conditions.
"They always try to find loopholes delaying them from lifting the embargo," Ma'Rouf said. The Security Council is the only body with the power to end sanctions.

"Some parties are saying we have not met requirements for dismantling mass weaponry. They are saying that there are... missiles still missing," he said. "Everything that needed to be destroyed has been destroyed."
"It is not in our interest to hide anything from the special commission."

The U.N. Security Council voted this month to keep the sanctions in place, meaning that the ban on the export of Iraqi oil and on most imports, except for food, medicine and other humanitarian items, remained in force.
A key condition for any lifting of the broad sanctions is a clean bill of health by the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of eliminating Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.
Ma'rouf told the summit in a speech on Friday that the embargo was crippling Iraq. Aid agencies also have said the country faces a tough winter because food and medicines are in short supply.
"The embargo imposed on Iraq has resulted in the destruction of the infrastructure of all the main sectors of production and services," he said.
Baghdad signed an agreement with the United Nations in May allowing it to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy food and medicine.
The pact was about to be implemented in September but was halted when Baghdad sent troops into northern Iraq to help one Kurdish faction fight another.
The five-day summit at the Rome headquarters of the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation ends on Sunday.
